chapters.title: Measuring the macroeconomy
chapters.summary: Gross domestic product counts the value of final goods and services, and can be measured three ways — by production, by spending and by income — which must agree. The expenditure identity and its rearrangement into saving equals investment are accounting truths that every model must respect. Real GDP, price indices and the unemployment rate turn raw data into the quantities macroeconomics explains, each with known blind spots.

items.name: GDP: the value of final output
items.pic: A toy economy of farmer, miller and baker: summing every sale double-counts, while summing value added or final sales gives the same GDP, shown as stacked bars.

items.name: Production, expenditure and income measures agree
items.pic: Edit transactions in the toy economy and three GDP meters (value added, final spending, factor incomes) move in lockstep; break the books with an unrecorded payment and they diverge.

items.name: The circular flow
items.pic: Households and firms exchanging goods, labour, income and spending as animated flows; add a government and a foreign sector and check that every node’s inflows equal its outflows.

items.name: The expenditure identity Y = C + I + G + NX
items.pic: A country’s GDP as a stacked bar of consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports over decades, with imports drawn below the axis.

items.name: Saving equals investment (and twin deficits)
items.pic: Rearrange the identity on screen: private saving plus public saving equals investment plus net capital outflow; raise the budget deficit and see which other term must give.

items.name: Real versus nominal GDP and the deflator
items.pic: Nominal GDP rises steeply while real GDP in base-year prices rises gently; their ratio, the deflator, is drawn, and changing the base year shifts real growth rates slightly.

items.name: The consumer price index
items.pic: Price a fixed basket over time; change the basket weights and see the measured inflation rate change, compared with the GDP deflator’s.

items.name: Unemployment and labour-force flows
items.pic: People flow between employed, unemployed and out of the labour force; the unemployment and participation rates are computed live, and discouraged workers lower the rate without anyone finding a job.

items.name: What GDP leaves out
items.pic: Countries ranked by GDP per head and by measures that add leisure, home production, inequality and environmental depletion; the rankings shift as you toggle each adjustment.

items.name: The hockey stick of world income
items.pic: GDP per head from year 1000 to today on linear and log axes for several regions: flat for centuries, then a sharp upturn after 1800 that began at different dates in different places.

chapters.title: The long run: production, labour markets and saving
chapters.summary: In the long run output is set by capital, labour and technology, and competitive factor markets divide it among them; with Cobb–Douglas technology the shares are constant, as they roughly are in the data. The labour market settles at a natural rate of unemployment determined by job flows, search frictions and wage setting. Households smooth consumption over time, which ties saving to interest rates and expected income.

items.name: The Cobb–Douglas aggregate production function
items.pic: Output as a surface over capital and labour with an α slider; doubling both inputs doubles output, while doubling capital alone runs into diminishing returns.

items.name: Factor shares are constant under Cobb–Douglas
items.pic: Pay each factor its marginal product: labour’s share stays at 1 − α whatever happens to K and L, overlaid on the U.S. labour share and its recent decline.

items.name: The loanable-funds market
items.pic: A downward investment-demand curve and a saving supply line; raise government purchases and the real interest rate rises, crowding out investment by the shaded amount.

items.name: Steady-state unemployment u = s/(s + f)
items.pic: Job-separation and job-finding rate sliders: simulated unemployment converges to s/(s + f), and the speed of convergence depends on s + f.

items.name: Search and matching and the Beveridge curve
items.pic: A matching function turns vacancies and job seekers into hires; the steady states trace the Beveridge curve, and an efficiency shock shifts it outward as after 2009.

items.name: Wage-setting and price-setting (WS–PS) equilibrium
items.pic: An upward wage-setting curve (efficiency wages) and a flat price-setting curve; they cross at equilibrium unemployment, which moves when you change markups or unemployment benefits.

items.name: The natural rate of unemployment
items.pic: Actual unemployment and estimated natural rates for several countries over time; frictional and structural components are shaded beneath.

items.name: Two-period consumption and saving (Fisher)
items.pic: A budget line between consumption today and tomorrow pivots with the interest rate; indifference curves locate the choice, and income and substitution effects are separated.

items.name: The permanent-income hypothesis
items.pic: A household’s income with transitory and permanent shocks: consumption responds almost fully to the permanent shock and barely to the transitory one.

items.name: The life-cycle hypothesis
items.pic: Income humps over working life while consumption stays flat; wealth accumulates then runs down in retirement, and an ageing population lowers national saving.

items.name: The consumption Euler equation
items.pic: Move a unit of consumption between periods: the marginal-utility trade-off is balanced only when u′(c₁) = β(1 + r)u′(c₂), and consumption growth is plotted against r.

items.name: Hall’s random walk of consumption
items.pic: Simulated consumption under rational expectations wanders like a random walk; lagged income has no predictive power in the regression readout.

items.name: Excess sensitivity and hand-to-mouth consumers
items.pic: Spending responses to predictable tax rebates by liquidity-constrained and unconstrained households, compared with a model mixing PIH and present-biased consumers.

items.name: A Theory of Production

paper.authors: Charles W. Cobb and Paul H. Douglas
paper.title: A Theory of Production

items.pic: Their indexes for US manufacturing, 1899–1922 (all 100 in 1899; by 1922 capital 431, labour 161, output 240), plotted against the fitted P = 1.01 L^¾ C^¼; drag the labour exponent and watch the fit worsen away from ¾, close to labour’s measured share of output, which was their argument for the formula.

chapters.title: Growth I: the Solow model
chapters.summary: Saving adds to the capital stock and depreciation wears it down, so with diminishing returns capital per worker converges to a steady state. Higher saving raises the level of income but not its long-run growth; only technological progress does that. The golden rule picks the saving rate that maximizes steady-state consumption, and the model predicts conditional convergence — poor countries with similar fundamentals should catch up — at a measurable speed.

items.name: Kaldor’s stylized facts of growth
items.pic: Long U.S. series for output per worker, capital per worker, the capital–output ratio, the real interest rate and labour’s share: two grow steadily, the rest are roughly flat.

items.name: The Solow–Swan model
items.pic: The saving curve s·f(k) and the break-even line δk; capital per worker evolves along the arrows between them, animated from any starting k you drag.

items.name: The steady state exists and is stable
items.pic: Plot k̇ against k: it is positive below the crossing and negative above, so every path converges; replace f with a technology that violates the Inada conditions and the steady state disappears.

items.name: The golden-rule saving rate
items.pic: Steady-state consumption against the saving rate is a hump; its peak is where the marginal product of capital equals depreciation, which for Cobb–Douglas means s = α.

items.name: Dynamic inefficiency
items.pic: Start above the golden rule and cut saving: consumption jumps immediately and stays higher forever, so oversaving makes every generation worse off.

items.name: Solow with population growth
items.pic: Add population growth n to the break-even line (n + δ)k; faster population growth lowers steady-state income per worker, shown against cross-country data.

items.name: Labour-augmenting technical progress and balanced growth
items.pic: With technology growing at g, capital per effective worker settles down while output per worker grows at g forever; log plots show the balanced-growth lines.

items.name: Speed of convergence
items.pic: Linearize around the steady state: the gap closes at rate (1 − α)(n + g + δ), about 4% a year for α = 1/3 — faster than the roughly 2% estimated from data.

items.name: Growth accounting and the Solow residual
items.pic: Decompose output growth into capital, labour and the residual for several countries and decades; the residual (TFP) carries much of the growth miracle.

items.name: Conditional versus absolute convergence
items.pic: Growth against initial income for all countries (no pattern) and for OECD members or after controlling for saving and population growth (a clear negative slope).

items.name: The Lucas paradox
items.pic: The Solow model’s implied return to capital in India versus the U.S. (dozens of times higher) against actual capital flows, which run the other way.

items.name: Harrod–Domar and the knife edge
items.pic: Fix the capital–output ratio: growth equals s/v, and unless it matches labour-force growth, unemployment or idle capital grows without bound — contrasted with Solow’s flexible version.

items.name: The productivity paradox (Solow)
items.pic: Computing investment soars while measured TFP growth stays flat until the late 1990s; a lag-and-learning toggle shows how a general-purpose technology can show up late.

items.name: A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth

paper.title: A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth

items.pic: Solow’s Figure 1: the saving curve sF(r, 1) against the ray nr, with r capital per worker; drag the saving rate, the population growth rate and the shape of the production function (his Cobb–Douglas and other examples) and watch r converge to the crossing from either side, the knife edge of Harrod–Domar replaced by a stable balanced path.

chapters.title: Growth II: optimal saving, ideas and history
chapters.summary: Making saving a choice gives the Ramsey model of optimal growth and the Diamond model of overlapping generations, which can oversave. To explain long-run growth itself, endogenous-growth theory treats ideas as non-rival goods produced by research. Before 1800 the economy behaved in a Malthusian way, with technology raising population rather than living standards, and today’s income gaps reflect institutions as well as capital and ideas.

items.name: Ramsey–Cass–Koopmans optimal growth
items.pic: Explore a Cobb–Douglas, CRRA optimal-growth model, including logarithmic utility at curvature one. Compare starting consumption with the computed stable arm through the exact steady state; finite off-arm time paths stop at the phase window or numerical cutoff.

items.name: The Diamond overlapping-generations model
refs: Acemoglu, MIT 14.452 Overlapping Generations (2018), slides 9–45; Diamond 1965 original model differs in depreciation
items.pic: Iterate the full-depreciation, log-utility saving map and compare competitive capital with golden-rule consumption. The gross return test identifies overaccumulation; an exact resource-gain example shows why appropriate transfers can benefit all cohorts.

items.name: The AK model
items.pic: Remove diminishing returns by making output linear in broad capital: the saving and break-even lines never cross, and the saving rate now changes the growth rate.

items.name: Romer’s endogenous growth: non-rival ideas
items.pic: Split labour between producing goods and researching ideas; because ideas are non-rival, the share in research sets the long-run growth rate, shown as diverging log paths.

items.name: Scale effects and the Jones critique
items.pic: The number of researchers has grown many-fold while U.S. growth stayed flat; a semi-endogenous model with diminishing research productivity matches both.

items.name: The Malthusian economy
items.pic: Income per head and population before 1800 with a land constraint: a technology improvement raises population density, not living standards, as the simulation returns to subsistence.

items.name: Escaping the Malthusian trap
items.pic: Raise the rate of technological progress past population’s maximum growth and add a demographic transition: income per head breaks away from subsistence, reproducing the hockey stick.

items.name: Human-capital-augmented Solow (Mankiw–Romer–Weil)
items.pic: Add schooling to the Solow regression: the fit to cross-country income improves and the implied capital share falls to plausible values.

items.name: Institutions as a fundamental cause (debated)
items.pic: Income against an institutions index, and the settler-mortality instrument with the critiques of its data; North and South Korea as a natural experiment in a side panel.

chapters.title: Money and inflation
chapters.summary: Money is whatever serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value; banks create most of it by lending. In the long run the quantity theory links money growth to inflation, the Fisher equation links inflation to nominal interest rates, and money is neutral for real variables. Governments that finance spending by printing money collect an inflation tax that, pushed too far, ends in hyperinflation.

items.name: The functions of money
items.pic: A barter economy needs a double coincidence of wants; add a commonly accepted good and the number of trades needed to reach everyone’s desired goods collapses, counted in the simulation.

items.name: Fractional-reserve banking and the money multiplier
items.pic: A deposit is lent, redeposited and lent again; the geometric series of deposits sums to 1/reserve-ratio, with a toggle for the endogenous-money view in which loans create deposits.

items.name: The quantity theory of money
items.pic: Money growth against inflation across countries over decades: points cluster around the 45° line, while year-to-year data in low-inflation countries scatter widely.

items.name: The Fisher equation
items.pic: Nominal rate, inflation and real rate as three linked sliders: i = r + π (exactly (1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + π)), with historical U.S. series and ex-ante versus ex-post real rates.

items.name: Monetary neutrality and the classical dichotomy
items.pic: Double the money supply in a flexible-price model: every price and wage doubles and every real quantity stays put, shown as two identical real panels.

items.name: Seigniorage and the inflation tax
items.pic: Revenue from money creation as a function of the inflation rate is a Laffer-type hump, because real money balances shrink as inflation rises.

items.name: The Cagan model of hyperinflation
items.pic: Money demand falling with expected inflation; finance a deficit beyond the seigniorage peak and the simulated price level explodes.

items.name: Hyperinflations: Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008
items.pic: Monthly price levels on a log axis for famous hyperinflations, with fiscal deficits and the stabilizations that ended them annotated.

items.name: The costs of inflation
items.pic: Separate the costs of expected inflation (shoe leather, menu costs, tax distortions) from unexpected inflation’s redistribution between lenders and borrowers, with sliders for each.

items.name: Money demand and liquidity preference
items.pic: Real money demand falls with the interest rate; shift money supply and the market interest rate moves along the demand curve.

chapters.title: The open economy in the long run
chapters.summary: In an open economy saving need not equal domestic investment; the gap is the current account. Exchange rates translate prices between countries; over long periods purchasing-power parity holds roughly, and interest-rate differences should be offset by expected currency movements. Both relationships fail in revealing ways — prices of non-traded goods rise with productivity, and high-interest currencies tend not to depreciate as predicted.

items.name: Current account, capital flows and the balance of payments
items.pic: A country’s saving and investment bars with the gap labelled as the current account; editing either one shows the matching capital inflow or outflow.

items.name: Nominal and real exchange rates
items.pic: Convert a basket priced in two currencies: the real exchange rate moves with the nominal rate and with relative inflation, with historical pairs plotted.

items.name: Purchasing-power parity
items.pic: Big Mac prices converted at market exchange rates; deviations from parity are large, and a long-run panel shows them shrinking only slowly over decades.

items.name: Uncovered interest parity
items.pic: Invest at home or abroad without hedging: the interest differential must equal expected depreciation; enter rates and an expected exchange-rate path to check.

items.name: The forward-premium puzzle and the carry trade
items.pic: Regress realized depreciation on interest differentials: the slope is near zero or negative instead of one, and a carry-trade strategy earns steady profits punctuated by crashes.

items.name: The small open economy with perfect capital mobility
items.pic: The world interest rate fixes investment; a domestic fiscal expansion now crowds out net exports instead of investment, shown in linked saving–investment and exchange-rate panels.

items.name: The Balassa–Samuelson effect
items.pic: Price levels against income per head across countries slope upward: productivity growth in traded goods raises wages and the prices of non-traded services, explained in a two-sector model.

chapters.title: The short run: the Keynesian cross and IS–LM
chapters.summary: When prices are sticky, output is set by demand. In the Keynesian cross, spending generates income that generates more spending, so a change in government purchases is multiplied; trying to save more can lower total saving. Adding the money market gives IS–LM, which shows how fiscal and monetary policy move output and interest rates — and why monetary policy loses traction at the zero lower bound.

items.name: Sticky prices and the short run
items.pic: Distribution of how long individual prices stay unchanged (magazines, haircuts, petrol); with sticky prices, a money increase raises output temporarily instead of prices.

items.name: The Keynesian consumption function
items.pic: Consumption against disposable income with an autonomous intercept and slope equal to the MPC; cross-section and long-run data show why Kuznets found the slope differs by horizon.

items.name: The Keynesian cross
items.pic: Planned expenditure crosses the 45° line at equilibrium income; a staircase of inventory adjustments shows output converging to it from any starting point.

items.name: The government-purchases multiplier 1/(1 − MPC)
items.pic: Raise government purchases by 1: rounds of re-spending stack up as a geometric series converging to 1/(1 − MPC), animated round by round.

items.name: Tax and balanced-budget multipliers
items.pic: A tax cut’s multiplier is −MPC/(1 − MPC); raising spending and taxes together leaves a balanced-budget multiplier of exactly one, confirmed on the cross.

items.name: The paradox of thrift
items.pic: Households try to save more: the expenditure line drops, income falls by the multiplier, and total saving ends unchanged (or lower when investment responds to income).

items.name: The IS curve
items.pic: Lower the interest rate in the upper panel’s investment function; the Keynesian cross shifts up, and the resulting (r, Y) points trace the downward IS curve below.

items.name: The LM curve
items.pic: Higher income raises money demand; with fixed money supply the interest rate must rise, tracing the upward LM curve from the money-market panel.

items.name: IS–LM equilibrium and policy
items.pic: Shift IS with fiscal policy and LM with monetary policy; output and interest rates move as the comparative statics predict, with crowding out shaded.

items.name: The liquidity trap and the zero lower bound
items.pic: With the LM curve flat at zero, monetary expansions slide along it without changing output while fiscal expansions keep full force; Japan after 1995 and the U.S. after 2008 annotated.

items.name: The multiplier–accelerator model (Samuelson)
items.pic: Investment responds to the change in output: the simulated economy oscillates, converges or explodes depending on the MPC and accelerator, mapped as regions of the parameter plane.

items.name: Tobin’s q and investment
items.pic: Market value of capital over its replacement cost against investment rates; q above one signals profitable investment, and adjustment costs set how fast firms respond.

items.name: Empirical fiscal multipliers (debated)
items.pic: Estimates from military build-ups, regional transfers and VARs plotted with intervals from 0.5 to 2; a toggle shows estimates rising in slumps and at the zero lower bound.

items.name: The Great Depression
items.pic: U.S. output, prices, money supply and bank failures 1929–1939 on linked axes; switch between the spending, money and debt-deflation explanations to see what each must explain.

items.name: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

paper.title: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

items.pic: The principle of effective demand of chapter 3: set the propensity to consume and the level of investment, and employment settles where aggregate demand meets aggregate supply, with nothing forcing that point to be full employment; then raise liquidity preference against a fixed money supply and watch the interest rate rise, investment fall and employment follow.

items.name: Mr. Keynes and the “Classics”

paper.title: Mr. Keynes and the “Classics”; A Suggested Interpretation

items.pic: Hicks’s own diagram: the IS curve (investment equals saving) and the LL curve (demand for money equals its supply) in the plane of income and interest; shift either with sliders, and stretch the flat left end of LL, where the rate cannot fall further, to see Hicks’s reading of Keynes’s “special theory”: monetary expansion stops working there while shifts of IS keep their full effect.

chapters.title: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
chapters.summary: The aggregate-demand curve summarizes IS–LM as a relation between prices and output. In the long run supply is vertical at potential output; in the short run it slopes upward because prices or information adjust slowly. Demand shocks move output temporarily; supply shocks force a choice between inflation and unemployment. Real-business-cycle theory instead explains fluctuations with flexible prices and technology shocks.

items.name: The aggregate-demand curve
items.pic: Lower the price level: real balances rise, LM shifts out and output rises, tracing the AD curve point by point from the IS–LM panel.

items.name: Long-run aggregate supply
items.pic: A vertical line at potential output determined by capital, labour and technology; shift AD and only prices change.

items.name: Short-run aggregate supply
items.pic: A sticky-price model in which a fraction of firms cannot reprice: the short-run supply curve’s slope flattens as that fraction rises, with the sticky-information variant beside it.

items.name: AD–AS dynamics: the return to potential
items.pic: Hit the economy with a demand shock: output jumps, then expected prices adjust period by period and the short-run curve drifts until output returns to potential.

items.name: Demand and supply shocks; stagflation
items.pic: Choose a shock — oil price, credit crunch, pandemic — and see AD or AS shift; supply shocks raise prices while lowering output, leaving policy a hard choice.

items.name: The Lucas islands model
items.pic: Producers see their own price but not the aggregate level; only the surprise part of money growth moves output, and the supply response shrinks as monetary noise grows.

items.name: Small menu costs, large welfare effects
items.pic: A firm’s profit is flat near its optimal price, so a small menu cost prevents repricing; the aggregate-demand externality makes the social loss much larger, shown as two curves.

items.name: Real-business-cycle model
items.pic: Technology shocks hit a flexible-price economy; simulated output, hours and consumption co-move like real data, and a panel compares their volatilities with U.S. statistics.

chapters.title: Inflation and unemployment
chapters.summary: Okun’s rule of thumb links output gaps to unemployment, and Phillips found that wage inflation was high when unemployment was low. Friedman and Phelps argued the trade-off is temporary because expectations adjust, a prediction the stagflation of the 1970s confirmed. How expectations are formed matters for the cost of disinflation and for the Lucas critique of policy evaluation; the Phillips curve’s recent flatness is debated.

items.name: Okun’s law
items.pic: Changes in unemployment against real GDP growth for the U.S.: a downward line with slope about −0.5; plot other countries and decades to see how unstable the coefficient is.

items.name: The original Phillips curve
items.pic: Phillips’s 1861–1957 U.K. data of wage inflation against unemployment, then the U.S. 1960s points along a similar curve.

items.name: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve
items.pic: A family of short-run Phillips curves indexed by expected inflation; keep unemployment below the natural rate and the curve ratchets upward each period.

items.name: NAIRU and the natural-rate hypothesis
items.pic: Only at the NAIRU is inflation stable; real-time NAIRU estimates are drawn with their wide bands and later revisions.

items.name: Adaptive versus rational expectations
items.pic: Announce a disinflation: adaptive forecasters lag behind, rational forecasters adjust immediately if they believe it, and the simulated unemployment costs differ accordingly.

items.name: The sacrifice ratio and disinflation
items.pic: The Volcker disinflation: cumulative output lost per point of inflation removed, compared with the textbook prediction and the rational-expectations ideal.

items.name: The stagflation of the 1970s
items.pic: U.S. inflation–unemployment points 1960–1985 connected in time order: the loops move up and right after the oil shocks, breaking the 1960s curve.

items.name: The flattening Phillips curve (debated)
items.pic: Slope estimates by decade fall toward zero, then the 2021–2023 inflation surge; toggle anchored expectations and supply shocks to see competing explanations.

items.name: Hysteresis in unemployment
items.pic: After a deep recession, long-term unemployed lose skills and attachment; simulated unemployment settles at a higher level, as in parts of Europe after the 1980s.

items.name: The Lucas critique
items.pic: Estimate a Phillips-curve trade-off from data generated under one policy rule, then exploit it: the relationship shifts as expectations adapt to the new rule.

items.name: Unemployment and the Rate of Change of Money Wage Rates

paper.title: The Relation between Unemployment and the Rate of Change of Money Wage Rates in the United Kingdom, 1861–1957

items.pic: Phillips’s Figure 1: the annual UK points for 1861–1913, his six averages by band of unemployment and the fitted curve y + 0.900 = 9.638x^−1.394, on which money wages are stable at about 5½% unemployment; step on to 1913–48 and 1948–57 to lay the later years over the old curve, and fit your own curve to any window of years.

items.name: The Role of Monetary Policy
items.pic: Use policy to hold unemployment below its natural rate: each year workers revise expected inflation from experience, the short-run Phillips curve shifts up, and holding the target takes ever-faster inflation; release the target and unemployment returns to the natural rate at whatever inflation expectations have reached, tracing Friedman’s vertical long-run curve.

items.name: Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique

paper.title: Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique
paper.venue: Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 1: 19–46

items.pic: Simulate an economy whose agents respond to the policy rule they expect: estimate a Phillips-curve regression on data generated under one monetary rule, switch the rule, and watch the estimated “structural” slope break while the deep parameters stay put, so that forecasts built on the old fit go wrong, as in Lucas’s examples.

chapters.title: Monetary and fiscal policy
chapters.summary: Modern central banks set an interest rate according to rules like Taylor’s, raising it more than one-for-one with inflation to stabilize the economy. Policymakers who can renege on promises face an inflation bias, which is why independent, inflation-targeting central banks emerged. Fiscal policy is constrained by the government budget constraint; Ricardian equivalence says debt-financed tax cuts should not stimulate, under strong assumptions.

items.name: The Taylor rule
items.pic: The federal funds rate since 1987 against the Taylor-rule prescription with sliders for its coefficients; the gaps in 2003–2005 and at the zero lower bound stand out.

items.name: The Taylor principle
items.pic: Set the inflation coefficient below or above one: the simulated economy’s inflation either spirals after a shock or returns to target, with the real rate’s response shown.

items.name: The dynamic AD–AS model
items.pic: Mankiw’s DAD–DAS curves in inflation–output space; impulse responses to demand, supply and policy shocks are plotted period by period.

items.name: The New Keynesian three-equation model
items.pic: Dynamic IS, New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy rule solved together; shocks produce impulse responses, and an indeterminacy region appears when the Taylor principle fails.

items.name: Time inconsistency and the inflation bias
items.pic: A policymaker who wants output above potential promises low inflation; once expectations are set, inflating pays, so the discretionary equilibrium has higher inflation and no output gain (Kydland–Prescott, Barro–Gordon).

items.name: Central-bank independence and inflation targeting
items.pic: Average inflation against an index of central-bank independence across countries, and inflation before and after the adoption of targeting regimes.

items.name: Policy lags and rules versus discretion
items.pic: Stabilize a simulated economy with a policy that acts with inside and outside lags; aggressive discretionary responses can amplify fluctuations, compared with a fixed rule.

items.name: Automatic stabilizers
items.pic: Make taxes proportional to income and add unemployment benefits: the multiplier shrinks and simulated output fluctuations are damped without any policy decision.

items.name: Government debt dynamics and r − g
items.pic: Debt-to-GDP evolves with the primary deficit and the gap between interest and growth rates; set r below g and even persistent deficits stabilize the ratio.

items.name: Ricardian equivalence
items.pic: A debt-financed tax cut today with the implied future tax: a forward-looking household saves the whole cut, while borrowing constraints, myopia or finite lives break the equivalence.

items.name: Tax smoothing (Barro)
items.pic: A temporary spending spike such as a war: financing it by debt and a permanent small tax rise has lower deadweight loss than a tax spike, as the convex-cost readout shows.

items.name: Quantitative easing and forward guidance
items.pic: At the zero lower bound the central bank buys long bonds and promises low future rates; the expected path of short rates and the long yield move in a term-structure panel.

items.name: Rules Rather than Discretion

paper.authors: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
paper.title: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans

items.pic: Their inflation–unemployment example: the policymaker’s indifference curves over a family of expectations-augmented Phillips curves; under discretion the economy settles where an indifference curve touches the curve that expectations have selected, with positive inflation and no less unemployment, while a binding rule reaches zero inflation at the same unemployment; raise the weight on unemployment and watch the inflation bias grow.

items.name: Discretion versus Policy Rules in Practice

paper.title: Discretion versus Policy Rules in Practice
paper.venue: Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 39: 195–214

items.pic: Taylor’s Figure 1: the federal funds rate, 1987–1992, against his rule r = p + 0.5y + 0.5(p − 2) + 2; drag the two weights and the 2% equilibrium real rate to see how closely each version tracks what the Fed actually did, then run the same rule over later years.

chapters.title: Open-economy macroeconomics in the short run
chapters.summary: With capital mobile across borders, the Mundell–Fleming model shows that fiscal policy works under fixed exchange rates and monetary policy under floating ones — and that a country cannot have free capital flows, a fixed exchange rate and independent monetary policy all at once. Exchange rates can overshoot after policy changes, fixed pegs can be attacked, and currency unions trade monetary independence for lower transaction costs.

items.name: Mundell–Fleming with floating exchange rates
items.pic: IS* and LM* curves in exchange-rate–output space: a fiscal expansion only appreciates the currency, while a monetary expansion depreciates it and raises output.

items.name: Mundell–Fleming with fixed exchange rates
items.pic: Fix the exchange rate: the central bank must accommodate fiscal expansions, which now raise output fully, while monetary policy is powerless.

items.name: The impossible trinity (trilemma)
items.pic: A triangle with free capital flows, fixed exchange rate and monetary autonomy at the corners; click a side to pick two and see the third break, with historical regimes placed on it.

items.name: Exchange-rate overshooting (Dornbusch)
items.pic: A permanent money increase with sticky prices: the exchange rate jumps past its new long-run level, then appreciates back as prices adjust, satisfying UIP along the way.

items.name: Speculative attacks on a peg
items.pic: A central bank financing deficits runs down reserves; speculators attack before reserves are exhausted, and the attack date is computed from the shadow exchange rate.

items.name: The Marshall–Lerner condition and the J-curve
items.pic: After a devaluation the trade balance first worsens, then improves once volumes respond; it improves overall only if export and import elasticities sum to more than one.

items.name: Optimal currency areas (Mundell)
items.pic: Two regions hit by asymmetric shocks: with a shared currency, adjustment must come from labour mobility, wage flexibility or fiscal transfers, each a slider.

chapters.title: Financial crises
chapters.summary: Banks transform short-term deposits into long-term loans, which makes them vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs. Leverage amplifies losses, falling asset prices tighten borrowing constraints, and debts fixed in nominal terms grow heavier as prices fall. Minsky argued that stability itself breeds the risk-taking that ends in crisis. Central banks act as lenders of last resort, and since 2008 the possibility of chronically weak demand has returned to the agenda.

items.name: Bank runs (Diamond–Dybvig)
items.pic: Depositors decide whether to withdraw early; if enough others run, running is optimal, so the simulation has a good and a bad equilibrium, and deposit insurance removes the bad one.

items.name: Leverage and the financial accelerator
items.pic: A bank with 30× leverage loses equity on a small asset decline, fire-sells assets, depresses prices further and hits other banks; a leverage slider shows when the spiral starts.

items.name: Debt deflation (Fisher)
items.pic: Falling prices raise real debt burdens, borrowers cut spending, prices fall further; the simulated loop is compared with 1929–1933 data.

items.name: Minsky’s financial instability hypothesis
items.pic: Over a long expansion, firms move from hedge to speculative to Ponzi financing; an agent model shows calm periods breeding the leverage that ends in a crash.

items.name: The 2007–2009 financial crisis
items.pic: House prices, mortgage defaults, interbank spreads and unemployment on linked timelines, with the policy responses annotated.

items.name: The lender of last resort (Bagehot)
items.pic: Lend freely against good collateral at a penalty rate: in the run simulation the central bank’s backstop stops the run with little lending actually used.

items.name: Tipping points and multiple equilibria in macro
items.pic: Investment depends on expected demand and demand on investment; the S-shaped response curve gives high and low equilibria, and a confidence shock tips the economy between them.

items.name: Secular stagnation (debated)
items.pic: The estimated natural real interest rate falling since the 1980s, with saving-glut, ageing and low-investment explanations as overlays and the post-2021 rise in rates added.

items.name: Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity

paper.authors: Douglas W. Diamond and Philip H. Dybvig
paper.title: Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity

items.pic: A bank holds a project that pays R > 1 at date 2 but only 1 if liquidated early, and promises depositors r₁ > 1 at date 1: set the share of impatient depositors and how many patient ones you expect to withdraw, and watch a patient depositor’s best response flip from waiting to running, giving one good equilibrium and one run; toggle suspension of convertibility or deposit insurance and the run equilibrium disappears.
